title: Navratri 2026: Devotional Bhajans for Nine Mornings of Maa Durga Worship
excerpt: Separate from the garba dance floor, here are the modern and classic bhajans for morning puja, aarti, and nine days of quiet devotion.
body:
• Sharad Navratri runs October 11-19, 2026, and the festival has two soundtracks. This is the devotional one: bhajans for morning puja, aarti, and quiet home worship, entirely separate from the garba dance floor.
  • The modern essentials come from playback singers turned devotional artists: Jubin Nautiyal's "Meri Maa Ke Barabar Koi Nahi," "Mai Balak Tu Mata," and "Maa Ka Bulawa Aaya Hai," plus Shreya Ghoshal's "Jab Jab Navratre Aave" and Sachet Tandon and Payal Dev's "Mai Ni Mai."
  • The classics that anchor every home are Anuradha Paudwal's "Jai Ambe Gauri" and "Ambe Tu Hai Jagdambe," Narendra Chanchal's "Chalo Bulawa Aaya Hai," and Mahendra Kapoor's "Durga Hai Meri Maa."
  • Reader utility: free curated playlists do the sequencing for you. JioSaavn's "Navratri-Jai Jagdambe" carries 40 tracks and its "Maa Durga - Devi Bhakti Bhajan" playlist runs 50 deep. Play the aarti block during morning puja, roughly 6-9 AM wherever you are, before the workday begins.

Two soundtracks, one festival

Navratri is famous for its noise: dhol drums, clapping sticks, ten thousand dancers moving in concentric circles past midnight. But the festival's other soundtrack begins at dawn, and it is the one most households actually live with. Before the garba grounds fill, families perform ghatasthapana, light the akhand jyot, and sing to the goddess. The devotional playlist of Sharad Navratri, which begins October 11, 2026, belongs to those hours: morning aarti, evening diya-lighting, and the nine days of fasting when many households keep music strictly devotional.

The modern devotional wave

A striking feature of recent Navratri seasons is how many mainstream playback singers now record bhajans as a parallel career. Jubin Nautiyal leads the field. "Meri Maa Ke Barabar Koi Nahi," his duet with Payal Dev, "Mai Balak Tu Mata," and "Maa Ka Bulawa Aaya Hai" (with Payal Dev and lyrics by Manoj Muntashir) have become fixtures of the morning-puja rotation, according to Bollywood Holic's roundup of the season's most-played Maa Durga bhajans. Sachet Tandon and Payal Dev's "Mai Ni Mai" and Shreya Ghoshal's "Jab Jab Navratre Aave" sit in the same tier: polished studio productions with the devotional directness of older bhajans. Tulsi Kumar's "Bhor Bhayi Din" captures the sunrise-temple feeling its title promises, while Parampara Tondon's "Lal Chunariya," Arijit Singh's "Maiya Teri Jai Jaikar," Vishal Mishra's "Maa Ka Mann," and Sonu Nigam's "Maa Mera Hath Pakadti Hai" round out a modern canon that did not exist a decade ago.

The classics every home knows

Underneath the new wave sit the bhajans no playlist can skip. Anuradha Paudwal's "Jai Ambe Gauri" and "Ambe Tu Hai Jagdambe" have been the default aarti closers for two generations. Narendra Chanchal's "Chalo Bulawa Aaya Hai," from the film Avtaar with music by Laxmikant-Pyarelal and lyrics by Anand Bakshi, remains the definitive call to the goddess. Mahendra Kapoor's "Durga Hai Meri Maa" and the Sanskrit stotras, from "Ya Devi Sarvabhuteshu" to the Mahishasura Mardini stotram, anchor the ritual end of the spectrum. The Daily Jagran's 90-bhajan Navratri compilation shows how deep this bench runs: "Meri Maiya Sherowali," "Pyara Saja Hai Dwaar Bhavani," and "Kabhi Durga Banke Kabhi Kaali Banke" have been sung in homes and pandals for decades.

A calmer way to start the day

There is a practical reason the devotional list matters beyond ritual. Many listeners use the morning bhajan block the way others use a meditation app: fifteen to twenty minutes of familiar, repetitive melody before the day's noise begins. During the nine fasting days, when households eat once and keep the home quiet, the bhajan playlist becomes the background of the entire week. Bollywood Holic's readers describe listening while working, noting that the combination of modern production and devotional lyrics settles the mind without demanding attention. It is not a medical claim; it is a household habit, and during Navratri it is a widespread one.

The diaspora angle

For Indian families abroad, the devotional playlist does heavier lifting than it does back home. There is no neighborhood pandal to walk to, no loudspeaker aarti drifting over the street at dawn. Streaming has become the substitute: a phone on the kitchen counter playing the aarti sequence while the diya is lit, children learning "Jai Ambe Gauri" from the same recording their grandparents sang. Homes in the US, UK, and Canada recreate ghatasthapana with what the phone can provide, and the phone provides a great deal.

What's next

The nine days honor nine forms of Durga, from Shailputri on Day 1 to Siddhidatri on Day 9, with the eighth and ninth days, Ashtami and Navami, bringing the heaviest aarti traffic of the festival. Dussehra follows on October 20. Build the devotional list once this weekend and it serves every morning through the festival. The dance playlist can wait until evening.
